# A sharp centroid bound when a cap crosses every interval fiber

Let C be a convex body in R x R, with mixed measure mu given by ordinary
length on its integer fibers. Let g be its TRUE unweighted mixed-volume
centroid. Its base coordinate need not be integer for the following cap
lemma. Let H be a nonvertical closed halfspace whose boundary contains g,
and suppose that boundary meets EVERY positive-length integer fiber.
Tangency at a fiber endpoint is permitted.

Then

    mu(H)/mu(S)>=(sqrt(3)-1)/2>1/4.                 (1)

The same bound holds for the opposite closed halfspace. Equality is
attained by an actual three-fiber convex body whose true centroid has
integer base. Thus the universal constant in this particular cap lemma
is sharp. It does not cover caps with positive fibers wholly on one side
of their boundary.

## 1. An exact norm bound for a finite concave sequence

If c_0,...,c_(N-1) is nonnegative, nonzero and concave, then

    N sum c_i^2 <= kappa_N^2 (sum c_i)^2,           (2)

where

    kappa_1=1, kappa_2=sqrt(2),
    kappa_N^2=2N(2N-3)/[3(N-1)(N-2)], N>=3.

Every displayed constant is sharp for the sequence problem. In particular
kappa_N<=sqrt(3) for every N, with equality only at N=3.

For N=1,2 the statement is immediate, with extremizers a singleton or a
sequence with one zero endpoint. For N>=3, the cone of nonnegative concave
sequences is generated by its two nonnegative affine endpoint sequences
and by the triangular tents

    T^j_i=i/j for i<=j,
          (N-1-i)/(N-1-j) for i>=j,  1<=j<=N-2.

Here is an explicit decomposition, avoiding an unproved extremal claim.
Subtract the affine interpolation of the endpoint values. If
Delta_j=2c_j-c_(j-1)-c_(j+1)>=0, the remainder equals

    sum_(j=1)^(N-2) Delta_j [j(N-1-j)/(N-1)] T^j.

Both sides have zero endpoints and the same second differences, so their
difference is an affine sequence with zero endpoints. All coefficients,
including those of the endpoint interpolation, are nonnegative.

After normalizing each nonzero sequence to have sum one, this decomposition
is a convex combination. Squared Euclidean norm is convex, so its maximum
is no larger than the largest normalized generator norm. An endpoint
generator has sum N/2 and squared norm N(2N-1)/[6(N-1)]. An interior tent,
with j+l=N-1, has

    sum T^j=(N-1)/2,
    sum (T^j)^2=(N-1)/3+(1/6)(1/j+1/l).

The latter is largest when j=1 or l=1. Comparing that value with the
endpoint value gives exactly (2), attained by T^1 or T^(N-2). Finally
kappa_N^2<=3 for N>=3 is equivalent to
5N^2-21N+18>=0, whose roots are 6/5 and 3. This proves all assertions.

## 2. The true centroid supplies equality of squared norms

Use the affine margin of H as a new continuous coordinate X, orienting
H={X>=0}. Its continuous coefficient is nonzero, so this is a
lattice-preserving affine shear and continuous rescaling; every fiber
length and the total mixed measure change by the same constant. The
transformed TRUE scalar centroid is exactly zero.

Positive-length integer fibers have consecutive indices, because their
length is a nonnegative concave function of the real base. Relabel them
0,...,N-1. By the crossing hypothesis their intervals are

    [-a_i,b_i],  a_i>=0, b_i>=0.

Both a_i and b_i are concave sequences: the upper endpoint of a convex
body is concave and the negative lower endpoint is concave. The scalar
centroid identity is

    0=sum_i integral_(-a_i)^(b_i) X dX
     =(1/2)sum_i(b_i^2-a_i^2).                     (3)

Let A=sum a_i and B=sum b_i. Neither is zero: otherwise (3) forces every
interval to have zero length. By Cauchy--Schwarz, (3), and (2),

    A<=sqrt(N sum a_i^2)
      =sqrt(N sum b_i^2)<=kappa_N B.

Since mu(H)/mu(S)=B/(A+B), this proves the stronger N-dependent bound

    mu(H)/mu(S)>=1/(1+kappa_N),                    (4)

and hence (1). Swapping a and b gives the same bound for the opposite cap.
All closed boundary sections have zero length, including the tangent
fibers allowed in the hypothesis.

Zero-length integer fibers, if present, carry no mu mass and can only lie
at the ends of the positive-length range. Restricting the concave endpoint
sequences to that range preserves concavity. Thus none were discarded from
the relevant moment equation or mass sum.

## 3. Sharpness with an integer-base true centroid

At indices -1,0,1 take the fibers

    [-1,0], [-1,sqrt(3)], [-1,0].

They are induced exactly by their full-dimensional convex hull. The base
centroid is zero by symmetry. The continuous first moment is
(1/2)[0^2+3+0^2-(1+1+1)]=0. Thus the actual mixed centroid is (0,0).
The closed cap {X>=0} meets each fiber, has mass sqrt(3), and the total
mass is 3+sqrt(3). Its normalized mass is

    sqrt(3)/(3+sqrt(3))=1/(1+sqrt(3))=(sqrt(3)-1)/2.

This proves sharpness of (1) in the original geometric class, with the
centroid belonging to S itself. No tilted or otherwise reweighted volume
is used. Replacing both endpoint upper heights by epsilon>0 and the middle
upper height by sqrt(3-2epsilon^2), with sufficiently small epsilon, keeps
the actual centroid at zero and makes all crossings strict. These bodies
approach the same sharp constant if touching is disallowed.

Consequently a conditional-centroid failure of the n=d=1 OC bound, if one
exists, must have a bad cap with a positive-length fiber wholly on one side
of its boundary. This is an exact restriction on that unresolved case,
not a proof that every minimizing cap crosses every fiber.
